Improvement Comments:
I think if the reading materials were covered better in class, the course would be much smoother.

In addition, the Hindi terminology needs to be spelled consistently (I've seen some terms spelled three different ways throughout the course), as well as to either be explained better (so students will learn it instead of simply learning how to regurgitate), or less emphasized. As it is now, the more specific and less used Hindi vocabulary is a matter of regurgitating the meaning, rather than explaining it. Instruments and general terms like 'tabla' and 'raga' are fine, but testing us on the name of the relation between Sa and Ma is more of a vocabulary question than a music theory question, and does not test our actual knowledge of the material.

While there's rarely anything gramatically wrong with them, they tend to incorporate terminology and phrasing that is awkward to most English-speakers like myself. Valuable Comments: What I found most valuable about this course was the immersive introduction to the theory and practice of Hindustani classical music. Learning about the structure of ragas, the role of improvisation, and the cultural and spiritual contexts of the music gave me a much deeper appreciation for its complexity and beauty. I especially valued the live demonstrations, whether through recordings or guest artists, which brought the theoretical material to life. The course struck a great balance between academic study and experiential learning, which made the subject both intellectually engaging and emotionally resonant. | Not one complaint, the professor told you exactly what she expected out of you and is very passionate about teaching.
